originalTitle: A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops

content: Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models. The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing. All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM. These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s a lot to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week. Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep? Does it just work? [Image: A laptop costing $7,000 better just work, and work well. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268814_Nvidia_RTX_Spark_Asus_ProArt_P16_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Antonio Di Benedetto: Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer. Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities. Sean Hollister: Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode. But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below. Tom Warren: I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming. Can it game? [Image: Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra during a Microsoft demo. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0229.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] TW: Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go. SH: Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in Returnal (at 1440p with high settings), Expedition 33 (at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings), Jedi Survivor (DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and Shadow of the Tomb Raider (at native 1800p and highest spec). But when I fired up Helldivers 2, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up. chineseContent: Nvidia 的 RTX Spark N1X 处理器终于问世了，我们一直在集体测试价值不菲的配备这款新“超级芯片”的强大笔记本电脑。 RTX Spark 旨在成为一款基于 Arm 的高性能 SoC，适用于笔记本电脑和小型台式电脑，可与 Apple、Intel、AMD 和 Qualcomm 的最佳产品相媲美。它拥有大量核心、Nvidia RTX Blackwell 显卡以及足够的功率和统一内存来运行大型本地 AI 模型。旗舰产品位于微软 Surface Laptop Ultra 中，具有惊人的 128GB 统一内存，我们自己的 Tom Warren 对此进行了全面评测。 Sean Hollister 一直在测试 64GB 版本的 Asus ProArt P16，我也在其顶级规格 128GB 配置中进行了测试。由于我是这群人中最被宠坏的，所以我还准备了一台 64GB 的 Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 和一台 32GB 的 HP OmniBook Ultra 来进行测试。所有这些笔记本电脑都配备相同的 N1X 芯片，具有 20 个 CPU 内核和 6,144 个 GPU CUDA 内核，而且价格都非常昂贵，从 HP OmniBook 的 3,199.99 美元到华硕 ProArt 的 6,999.99 美元。有一个成本较低的 18 核 / 5,120 CUDA N1X 芯片配置，但对于 Surface Laptop Ultra 或具有 24GB RAM 的较小的 Asus ProArt P14 来说，它的价格仅为 2,599.99 美元。这些是基于新芯片的大型且昂贵的笔记本电脑。它们面向开发人员、编码人员和内容创作者，他们可能还希望能够使用本地 AI，甚至使用最新的 Nvidia 技术（如 DLSS 5）玩游戏。有很多东西需要测试，但我们没有太多时间来测试所有这些。因此，下面您不会找到对任何一台笔记本电脑的详尽评分评论，而是来自三位作家使用五台笔记本电脑一周的印象和想法。英伟达的“超级芯片”真的那么超级吗？ Apple、Intel、AMD 和 Qualcomm 是否已正式发出通知？有我们任何一个人
